messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 38
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Teacher
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 56

He is thirty-eight, European, married, and has spent most of his adult life in classrooms. Before the robbery, he thinks of himself as the kind of teacher who stays late to stack marked essays into neat piles, who knows which student needs a joke before a test and which one needs quiet encouragement. His days are organized by bells, lesson plans, and the dependable rhythm of school terms. He likes routine. His wife teases him about the way he lines up his shoes by the door and checks the locks before bed, but it is an affectionate joke, part of the ordinary life they have built together.

The robbery happens on a wet Thursday in November. He has stayed after school for parent conferences and leaves later than usual, carrying a satchel full of exercise books and a laptop the school has issued him. The streets are not empty, but they are dim and slick with rain. He cuts through a side street he has taken dozens of times. He hears footsteps behind him and at first barely notices. Then someone grabs the strap of his bag hard enough to jerk him backward. He turns and sees two young men in hooded sweatshirts. One shouts at him to give it over. The other steps in close and presses something cold and metallic against his ribs. To this day he is not fully sure whether it is a knife or only something meant to feel like one, but in that moment his body knows only danger.

He remembers strange details more clearly than the whole: the smell of stale smoke on one of them, the shine of water on the pavement, his own breath suddenly loud in his ears. He hands over the bag, but one of them shoves him down anyway. His shoulder hits the ground, and his face strikes the pavement with enough force to split the inside of his lip. They run. For a few seconds he cannot move. He lies there stunned, hearing footsteps disappear and feeling a humiliating wave of helplessness unlike anything he has known before.

In the first days afterward, he tells the story as if it is unpleasant but contained. The police take a statement. His wife insists he go to urgent care for the bruising and the shoulder pain. Colleagues at school are sympathetic, and he shrugs it off with a brittle kind of humor. He says he was unlucky. He says at least they only took his bag. At night, though, he jerks awake drenched in sweat, convinced someone is in the room. In one dream he is back on the pavement, unable to breathe. In another he hears footsteps behind him and cannot make his legs move. His wife reaches for him and he startles so violently that she pulls her hand back.

Over the following weeks, his world narrows. He cannot walk down that side street, then cannot walk anywhere alone after dark, then begins avoiding even the train station where commuters bunch too close behind him. On his commute he scans faces, especially young men in dark hoodies, and feels ashamed of the suspicion that rises in him automatically. If someone steps too near, his body stiffens before his mind catches up. He begins taking a much longer route to school, leaving home earlier and arriving already tired.

In the classroom he is still competent, but less available. A slammed door makes his heart pound so hard he loses his place mid-sentence. When boys at the back of the class start whispering and laughing, he finds himself watching their hands, their posture, calculating risk before he can hear their words. Once, when a student comes up behind him unexpectedly while he is writing on the board, he spins around sharply enough to frighten them both. He apologizes, then spends the rest of the lesson feeling exposed and shaky. He used to enjoy staying after school to help students one-to-one, but now he leaves as soon as he can, uneasy in the building once the corridors empty out.

At home, his wife notices that he checks the front door repeatedly, then the windows, then the door again. He says he is just being careful. He stops carrying his school laptop if he can avoid it. He leaves his satchel in a cupboard because the sight of the torn replacement strap reminds him too much of that night. When his wife suggests meeting friends for dinner in town, he makes excuses about marking or being tired. Crowded restaurants, loud bars, even the jostling at a weekend market all seem to demand more vigilance than he can sustain. He drinks more wine in the evenings than he used to, not enough to cause arguments, but enough that he recognizes he is trying to dampen something down.

What troubles him most is not only fear but the change in how he sees himself. He replays the moment on the pavement and thinks, absurdly but persistently, that he should have done something different. He should have noticed sooner, shouted louder, fought back, protected himself. He knows, rationally, that handing over the bag may have saved him from worse harm, but the knowledge does not touch the feeling. He feels diminished. In staff meetings, while others discuss curriculum and exam targets, he drifts back to the cold pressure at his ribs and the helpless certainty that his life could have ended in an ordinary side street on an ordinary evening.

Months later, the bruises are long gone, but his body still behaves as if the robbery is waiting to happen again. He sleeps lightly, waking at small noises. He sits in cafés facing the door. He times his journeys to avoid darkness and grows irritable when plans change at the last minute. His wife says she misses the ease he used to bring into a room. He misses it too. He still teaches, still marks papers, still tells himself each morning that he is fine. But underneath the routines that once steadied him, he lives with a constant sense of threat, as if the world has lost a basic promise of safety and has not given it back.
